query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of a segregating dopant (e.g., boron) during processing will improve both the tensile strength and room-temperature ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys by enhancing cohesion at the internal lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that have numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor dopant (such as boron) into the alloy system during processing so as to promote its segregation at the interfaces between the lamellar phases.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading on alloys processed to maintain the lamellar colony morphology; processing conditions must favor dopant segregation without forming unwanted second phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, segregated dopant layer (complexion) at the lamellar colony boundaries that increases interfacial cohesion.
generation.mechanism: The dopant segregation at internal boundaries enhances interfacial bonding, reducing local stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation. This improvement in boundary cohesion enables better dislocation transmission and work hardening, thereby simultaneously boosting tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the doped alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in tensile strength along with an improvement in ductility (higher elongation before failure) under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy produced via conventional processing, characterized by dual-phase lamellar colonies that suffer from early onset microcracking at poorly bonded internal boundaries, resulting in high strength but limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The efficacy of the intervention hinges on the dopant effectively segregating to the lamellar boundaries without forming deleterious phases. The hypothesis is most applicable to high-entropy alloys with a well-defined lamellar microstructure and may not extend to systems where the dopant distribution cannot be controlled.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal dopant concentration, the precise kinetics of dopant segregation under varied processing conditions, and the universality of the effect across different alloy compositions remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed with a minor boron addition intended to promote dopant segregation at the colony boundaries, and a control set without the dopant. Use identical thermal-mechanical processing conditions to ensure comparable lamellar colony formation. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural examinations (via TEM/EDS) to assess dopant segregation at the interfaces.
measurements: Interfacial composition and segregation via microscopy and spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not result in a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if no dopant segregation is detected at the lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.
